"title": "The structural basis for regulation of the glutathione transporter Ycf1 by regulatory domain phosphorylation",
"authors": "Nitesh Kumar Khandelwal; Cinthia R Millan; Samantha I Zangari; Samantha Avila; Dewight Williams; Tarjani M Thaker; Thomas M Tomasiak",
"field_subfield": "Structural biology / membrane transport (ABCC transporters)",
"type_of_paper": "Structural and biochemical study",
"executive_summary": "Yeast Cadmium Factor-1 (Ycf1) is an ATP-binding cassette C-subfamily (ABCC) transporter that sequesters glutathione and heavy metals into the vacuole to protect cells from oxidative and metal stress. Its activity is thought to be regulated by phosphorylation on an intrinsically disordered regulatory domain (R-domain), but the structural basis of this regulation had not been resolved because prior structures only captured short, unassigned R-domain fragments. Here, the authors used cryo-electron microscopy to determine two structures of endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1 at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolution, representing wide (IFwide) and narrow (IFnarrow) inward-facing conformations. These structures were obtained from an E1435Q NBD2 Walker B mutant, which substantially lowered ATPase activity and allowed trapping of these conformations. The key finding is that the R-domain (residues 901-935) is resolved in an ordered, helical state and is phosphorylated at three sites (S908, T911, S914), forming an extensive interaction interface with NBD1 and the lasso domain. These interactions are nearly constant between the two states, related by rigid-body movements of the NBD1/R-domain complex relative to NBD2. Biochemical experiments show that dephosphorylation increases protease accessibility and drastically reduces ATPase activity, indicating that R-domain phosphorylation is required for maximal ATPase activity. The work provides long-sought insights into how R-domains control ABCC transporter activity and challenges the widely held model of CFTR activation, which proposes R-domain release upon phosphorylation. The authors propose instead that phosphorylation drives R-domain association with NBD1, stabilizing a primed, active state. The study also rationalizes clinically relevant findings, such as the effect of mutations distal to phosphorylation sites and the binding of the CFTR corrector lumacaftor near the R-domain binding site. This work establishes a defined binding site for the conserved R-domain and suggests implications for allosteric modulation of transporters with long phosphorylated domains.",

Many ABCC transporters are regulated by phosphorylation on intrinsically disordered regulatory domains (R-domains), but the mechanism remains poorly understood. Here the authors report two cryo-EM structures of endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1 at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolution, captured in two inward-facing conformations designated IFwide and IFnarrow. These structures reveal a previously unobserved ordered state of the R-domain (residues 901-935), which is phosphorylated at three sites (S908, T911, S914). The phosphorylated R-domain encircles NBD1 and interacts extensively with NBD1, the lasso domain, and the TMDs through electrostatic, hydrogen-bonding, and hydrophobic contacts that bury substantial surface area. Biochemical experiments show that dephosphorylation increases protease accessibility and drastically reduces ATPase activity, indicating that R-domain phosphorylation stabilizes an architecture that facilitates ATP hydrolysis. The authors propose a model in which phosphorylation drives the R-domain from an unbound/disordered state to a bound/ordered state near NBD1, priming the transporter for transport. These findings provide long-sought insights into how R-domains control ABCC transporter activity and may inform understanding of related human transporters such as CFTR and MRP1.",

summary.title: The structural basis for regulation of the glutathione transporter Ycf1 by regulatory domain phosphorylation
summary.authors: Nitesh Kumar Khandelwal, Cinthia R Millan, Samantha I Zangari, Samantha Avila, Dewight Williams, Tarjani M Thaker, Thomas M Tomasiak
summary.executive_summary: Yeast Cadmium Factor-1 (Ycf1) is an ATP-binding cassette C-subfamily (ABCC) transporter that sequesters glutathione and heavy metals into the vacuole to protect cells from oxidative and metal stress. Many ABCC transporters are regulated by phosphorylation on intrinsically disordered regulatory domains (R-domains), but the mechanism remains poorly understood. Here the authors report two cryo-EM structures of endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1 at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolution, captured in two inward-facing conformations designated IFwide and IFnarrow. These structures reveal a previously unobserved ordered state of the R-domain (residues 901-935), which is phosphorylated at three sites (S908, T911, S914). The phosphorylated R-domain encircles NBD1 and interacts extensively with NBD1, the lasso domain, and the TMDs through electrostatic, hydrogen-bonding, and hydrophobic contacts that bury substantial surface area. Biochemical experiments show that dephosphorylation increases protease accessibility and drastically reduces ATPase activity, indicating that R-domain phosphorylation stabilizes an architecture that facilitates ATP hydrolysis. The authors propose a model in which phosphorylation drives the R-domain from an unbound/disordered state to a bound/ordered state near NBD1, priming the transporter for transport. These findings provide long-sought insights into how R-domains control ABCC transporter activity and may inform understanding of related human transporters such as CFTR and MRP1.

claims.description: R-domain phosphorylation stabilizes an ordered R-domain architecture that facilitates ATP hydrolysis in Ycf1.
The ordered R-domain architecture is stimulatory and does not support the model where CFTR activation depends on R-domain release.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Yeast Cadmium Factor-1 (Ycf1) is an ATP-binding cassette C-subfamily (ABCC) transporter that sequesters glutathione and heavy metals into the vacuole to protect cells from oxidative and metal stress. Many ABCC transporters are regulated by phosphorylation on intrinsically disordered regulatory domains (R-domains), but the mechanism remains poorly understood. Here the authors report two cryo-EM structures of endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1 at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolution, captured in two inward-facing conformations designated IFwide and IFnarrow. These structures reveal a previously unobserved ordered state of the R-domain (residues 901-935), which is phosphorylated at three sites (S908, T911, S914). The phosphorylated R-domain encircles NBD1 and interacts extensively with NBD1, the lasso domain, and the TMDs through electrostatic, hydrogen-bonding, and hydrophobic contacts that bury substantial surface area. Biochemical experiments show that dephosphorylation increases protease accessibility and drastically reduces ATPase activity, indicating that R-domain phosphorylation stabilizes an architecture that facilitates ATP hydrolysis. The authors propose a model in which phosphorylation drives the R-domain from an unbound/disordered state to a bound/ordered state near NBD1, priming the transporter for transport. These findings provide long-sought insights into how R-domains control ABCC transporter activity and may inform understanding of related human transporters such as CFTR and MRP1.

Research Context
ABC transporters regulate diverse molecules for lipid homeostasis, ion transport, and detoxification. Ycf1 transports glutathione and heavy metals into vacuoles to counter cell stress. Many ABCC transporters are regulated by phosphorylation on intrinsically disordered domains. The regulatory mechanism of R-domain phosphorylation is still poorly understood. Prior cryo-EM structures show a mostly disordered R-domain without assigned phosphorylation sites.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study seeks to determine the structural basis for R-domain phosphorylation regulation of Ycf1. The authors hypothesize that R-domain phosphorylation induces an ordered state that stabilizes interactions with NBD1 and the lasso domain. The authors predict that phosphorylation reorganizes Ycf1 architecture and is required for maximal ATPase activity. The authors predict that dephosphorylation increases protease accessibility and reduces ATPase activity. The authors predict that phosphorylation drives the R-domain from unbound/disordered to bound/ordered.

Methodological Details
The study used two forms of S. cerevisiae DSY5 strain: wild-type and the NBD2 Walker B mutant E1435Q. The YCF1 gene was cloned into the p423_GAL1 vector as an N-terminal Flag and C-terminal decahistidine fusion. The DSY-5 strain has genotype MATa leu2 trp1 ura3-52 his3 pep4 prb1. A 50 mL primary culture was grown for 24 hours at 30°C with shaking at 200 rpm in SC-His media. A secondary 750 mL culture was inoculated with 2% of the primary culture (15 mL). The culture was grown for an additional 16 hours at 30°C prior to harvesting. Cells were harvested by centrifugation at 5000xg for 30 minutes at 4°C. The lysis buffer contained 50 mM Tris-Cl pH 8.0, 300 mM NaCl, and cOmplete, EDTA-free protease inhibitor. The E1435Q dataset was processed in RELION (3.0 and 3.1) and cisTEM. Drift correction was performed using MotionCor2 with a pixel size of 1.031 Å/pixel. The CTF was estimated using CTFFIND4.1 prior to particle picking. An initial model was built using the SWISS-MODEL server and 6jb1 as a template. Manual model building was performed in COOT. Real-space refinement was performed in Phenix with CCP-EM modules for map sharpening/blurring. Evolutionary coupling analysis was performed using the Evcouplings package with PLMC. A total of 13,723 sequences were identified for evolutionary coupling analysis. ATPase rates were determined at 30°C using an enzyme-coupled assay. Each ATPase reaction consisted of 75 µL volumes containing 6.45 µg of protein. The absorbance was measured every minute at 340 nM for 30-45 min on a Synergy Neo2 reader. Kinetic parameters were derived using nonlinear regression in GraphPad Prism 9. Phosphorylation was assayed by in-gel phosphoprotein staining with Pro-Q Diamond. Dephosphorylated Ycf1 was generated by treating SEC-purified Ycf1 with Lambda phosphatase for 45 min at 4°C. Equal quantities (5 µg) of untreated and lambda PP treated samples were separated on 10% SDS-PAGE gels. LC-MS/MS analysis used Scaffold Q+S v 4.11.1 with a minimum of two peptides at 95% confidence. Limited proteolysis used trypsin from bovine pancreas at varying concentrations (0, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, and 15 µg/mL). Fixed amounts of Lambda PP treated and untreated Ycf1 protein (12 µg) were incubated for 30 min on ice. The reaction was stopped by adding 1 µg/mL of soybean trypsin inhibitor and incubating for an additional 15 min.

Procedures And Architectures
The E1435Q mutant resulted in substantially lowered ATPase activity, likely allowing the trapping of conformations. The WT Ycf1 ATPase Vmax was 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg. The structures revealed 17 transmembrane helices of TMD1 and TMD2, the accessory TMD0, the lasso motif, both NBDs, and a major portion of the R-domain. The two states are defined by differences in interdomain distances between the NBDs and the TMDs. The state in which the NBDs are further apart was designated IFwide. The state in which the NBDs are closer was designated IFnarrow. The unoccluded substrate cavities in both structures are large enough to accommodate oxidized glutathione (GSSG). The R-domain comprises residues 901-935 and is phosphorylated in three positions. The R-domain is helical (residues 920-929) in the C-terminal segment and lacks secondary structure in other regions. Phosphorylation was assigned to S908, T911, and S914 based on additional electron potential density. S908 is part of a recognition motif for PKA-like kinases called the RRAS motif. T911 serves as part of a CKII kinase recognition motif (S/T-(x)n-S/T). The phosphorylation sites form a scaffold that engages NBD1 and the lasso motif along a single axis. The hydrophobic surfaces bury ~1530 Å² and ~1338 Å² of surface area along the entire R-domain in IFnarrow and IFwide. The R-domain/NBD1 interface buries ~523 Å² (IFnarrow) and ~480 Å² (IFwide) specifically between NBD1 and the R-domain. The change in angle between residues G913, G918, and G932 of the R-domain was from 130º (IFwide) to 137.5º (IFnarrow). The glycines G918 and G932 cap the helical R-domain region and act as a hinge for movement. The second site in NBD2 (active) is open for ATP binding in IFnarrow. A third, less well-resolved state was called IFtransition and was insufficiently detailed to enable model building. Dephosphorylated Ycf1 showed a clear increase to protease accessibility with more complete digestion. ATPase assays showed a drastic activity reduction in dephosphorylated Ycf1. The concentration of ATP was held constant at 1 mM in substrate-stimulated ATPase activity experiments. EC50 and Vmax values were derived using nonlinear regression in GraphPad Prism 9.

Key Results
Two cryo-EM structures of Ycf1 were determined at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolution in distinct inward-facing conformations. The E1435Q mutant yielded homogenous particles from which two inward-facing conformations were identified. The structures revealed a previously unobserved ordered state of the R-domain. The R-domain is phosphorylated at three positions: S908, T911, and S914. Mass spectrometry and phosphostaining analysis confirmed phosphorylation at these three sites in both WT and E1435Q Ycf1. The phosphorylated R-domain encircles NBD1 and is stabilized by extensive contacts along a basic groove of the NBD1 perimeter. The interactions bury ~1530 Å² and ~1338 Å² of surface area along the entire R-domain in IFnarrow and IFwide. The R-domain/NBD1 interface buries ~523 Å² (IFnarrow) and ~480 Å² (IFwide) specifically between NBD1 and the R-domain. The change in angle between residues G913, G918, and G932 was from 130º (IFwide) to 137.5º (IFnarrow). The second site in NBD2 (active) is open for ATP binding in IFnarrow. Dephosphorylated Ycf1 showed a clear increase to protease accessibility with more complete digestion. The WT Ycf1 ATPase Vmax was 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg. ATPase assays showed a drastic activity reduction in dephosphorylated Ycf1. The E1435Q mutant resulted in substantially lowered ATPase activity compared to WT Ycf1. S908 is part of a recognition motif for PKA-like kinases called the RRAS motif. T911 serves as part of a CKII kinase recognition motif (S/T-(x)n-S/T). The R-domain and lasso domain phosphorylation may be inhibited by S251 phosphorylation through charge repulsion. The binding site of lumacaftor binds in the outer perimeter of NBD1 near the R-domain binding site.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The phosphorylated R-domain forms a scaffold that engages NBD1 and the lasso motif along a single axis. The extensive interactions between the phosphorylated R-domain and the rest of Ycf1 represent a stimulatory R-domain architecture. The authors propose a model where the R-domain transitions from unbound/disordered to bound/ordered upon phosphorylation. Phosphorylation along the R-domain drives association with the periphery of NBD1. The R-domain interactions lend a regulatory effect analogous to that of a transmission clutch. The findings do not support the model where CFTR activation depends on release of the R-domain. The results may provide implications for several other types of transporters where long phosphorylated unstructured domains are widespread. The presence of a single defined binding site for the conserved part of the R-domain confirms an anticipated but elusive binding site. The results suggest that phosphorylation helps stabilize NBD1 to recruit other domains into a conformation suitable for ATP binding. The results rationalize key clinically relevant findings related to other ABCC family members.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors note that the phosphates themselves may block protease accessibility to some sites. The authors note that their structures do not rule out an inhibitory role for the unphosphorylated state. The authors note that the R-domain mechanism has multiple competing models. The IFtransition state was insufficiently detailed to enable model building. The authors note that the structures were determined in apo conditions, not with substrate bound. The authors note that the R-domain phosphorylation does not induce activity alone, consistent with CFTR. The authors note that the structures do not resolve the phosphorylation sites in previous ABCC structures. The authors note that the R-domain mechanism is still debated in the field.

Claims
R-domain phosphorylation stabilizes an ordered R-domain architecture that facilitates ATP hydrolysis in Ycf1. The structures reveal a previously unobserved ordered state of the R-domain. The phosphorylated R-domain encircles NBD1 and is stabilized by extensive contacts. The interactions bury substantial surface area along the entire R-domain. ATPase assays show a drastic activity reduction in dephosphorylated Ycf1. Phosphorylation along the R-domain drives association with the periphery of NBD1. The authors note that the phosphates themselves may block protease accessibility to some sites. The authors note that the structures do not rule out an inhibitory role for the unphosphorylated state. The authors note that the R-domain mechanism has multiple competing models. The findings provide long-sought insights into how R-domains control ABCC transporter activity. The results may provide implications for several other types of transporters where long phosphorylated unstructured domains are widespread. The presence of a single defined binding site could provide a basis for allosteric modulation of transporter function.
The ordered R-domain architecture is stimulatory and does not support the model where CFTR activation depends on R-domain release. The extensive interactions between the phosphorylated R-domain and the rest of Ycf1 represent a stimulatory R-domain architecture. Our findings here do not support the model where CFTR activation depends on release of the R-domain. The R-domain transitions from unbound/disordered to bound/ordered upon phosphorylation. The authors note that the structures do not rule out an inhibitory role for the unphosphorylated state. The authors note that the R-domain mechanism is still debated in the field. The findings inform on how ABCC transporters are regulated. The results may provide implications for several other types of transporters where long phosphorylated unstructured domains are widespread.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study used two forms of S. cerevisiae DSY5 strain: wild-type and the NBD2 Walker B mutant E1435Q. The E1435Q mutant resulted in substantially lowered ATPase activity, likely allowing the trapping of conformations. The WT Ycf1 ATPase Vmax was 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg. The structures were determined in apo conditions, not with substrate bound. The IFtransition state was insufficiently detailed to enable model building. The authors note that the phosphates themselves may block protease accessibility to some sites. The authors note that the structures do not rule out an inhibitory role for the unphosphorylated state.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the cryo-EM structures of IFwide and IFnarrow states. Figure 2 shows the R-domain phosphorylation and its interactions. Figure 3 shows the hydrophobic surfaces that stabilize the R-domain NBD interaction. Figure 4 shows the different NBD orientation with a single-occluded ATP site in IFnarrow. Supplementary Table S1 shows the sequence conservation of the R-domain. Supplementary Table S2 shows the phosphorylation sites. Figure S1 shows the cloning, expression, and purification. Figure S7 shows the evolutionary coupling analysis. Figure S8 shows the comparison with MRP1.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: The study provides the first structures of an intact, endogenously phosphorylated R-domain with NBD1, revealing a stimulatory R-domain architecture. 2. The strongest evidence: The biochemical data showing a drastic reduction in ATPase activity in dephosphorylated Ycf1 supports the role of R-domain phosphorylation in stabilizing the active architecture. 3. The future path: The findings may provide implications for several other types of transporters where long phosphorylated unstructured domains or loops are widespread.
